contentHtml:
Summary

To export Notion pages to Word (DOCX) while maintaining collaboration, you can use several methods since Notion does not offer a direct export option. The most effective approaches include using a Notion AI agent to create a DOCX file, connecting an AI client through Notion MCP, or exporting the page as a PDF or Markdown and converting it to Word. After exporting, you can utilize ONLYOFFICE Document Editor for real-time collaboration on the resulting document.

  • Use Notion AI agent for high fidelity DOCX.
  • Connect AI clients via Notion MCP for flexibility.
  • Export as PDF/Markdown and convert to Word.
  • ONLYOFFICE enables collaborative editing of DOCX files.
  • Keep original Notion page editable and shareable.

Notion doesn’t currently offer a native “Export to Word” option, but there are several ways to turn a Notion page into an editable DOCX file. Here’s how each method works, and how to keep collaborating on the resulting document afterward.

Exporting a Notion page usually comes up for a reason: a client wants a Word file, a reviewer only works in Word’s track changes, or content needs to leave Notion entirely and live as a standalone document from here on. Notion wasn’t built for that kind of handoff, but there are now several ways to get the content into an editable DOCX file, depending on the tools you have available.

Why Notion doesn’t export straight to DOCX

Notion’s native export, available from the ••• menu on a page, currently offers PDF, HTML, and Markdown & CSV. DOCX isn’t one of the native export formats. Notion pages use a block-based structure, while DOCX follows a different document model, so turning a complex page into a Word document isn’t always a straightforward format conversion.

For more complex pages, an AI agent can take the page content and rebuild it as a structured document rather than simply converting the underlying blocks.

Three ways to get a Notion page into Word format

Let’s have a look at the available options we have today.

1. Ask a Notion AI agent to build the file

Since the Notion 3.6 update on July 1, 2026, Notion Agents can create downloadable files, including DOCX documents, based on instructions you give them. To use it, ask the agent to turn the page into a Word document and specify how you want the content structured. For example:

“Turn this page into a formatted Word document (.docx). Keep the headings, tables, bullet lists, and overall structure.”

The agent uses the page content to build a downloadable document. For pages with headings, tables, lists, and other structured content, this can be more convenient than exporting to PDF and converting the result afterward. Notion Agent is available on Business and Enterprise plans.

2. Connect an AI client through Notion MCP

Notion MCP lets compatible AI clients, including Claude and other supported tools, access content in your Notion workspace. You can use a Notion page as context and ask the AI client to create a DOCX outside Notion.

The exact workflow, available features, and plan requirements depend on the AI client and your Notion workspace settings.

3. Export to PDF/Markdown and convert it to Word

The simplest option doesn’t require AI: export the page as a PDF or Markdown from the ••• menu, then open the document using a converter. Word converts the PDF into an editable document and attempts to preserve its original layout, although complex tables, graphics, and other elements may not convert perfectly.

For a short, simple page, copying the content directly into Word may be just as quick.

Once you have the DOCX, keep it editable and collaborative

Whichever method you use, the resulting DOCX is a separate file from the original Notion page, and changes made to it won’t automatically sync back to Notion. The original page can still be edited and shared in real time, but the exported Word document follows its own editing workflow from that point on.

If the Word file itself now needs to be reviewed, edited, or updated by a team, you’ll need a collaborative document editor that works with DOCX files. That’s where ONLYOFFICE Document Editor comes in: the exported file opens exactly as a DOCX, with formatting intact, and from there it works like a normal collaborative document: real-time co-editing so a team can work on the same file at once, comments for feedback, track changes for review, and version history to see what changed and roll it back if needed.

The suite is open source and free to self-host on your own server, and it also connects to over 40 platforms, including Moodle, ownCloud, and WordPress, so the file can be opened and edited online inside whatever system a team already uses, without a separate app in the loop.

If the export left behind rough edges, an orphaned heading, inconsistent list formatting, a paragraph that reads like it was translated twice, ONLYOFFICE’s AI Tools can clean that up inside the same window: rewriting a paragraph, fixing tone, or reformatting a section, with support for OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek, and other providers, so the choice of model isn’t locked in.

Comparing the three export methods

Method Needs Output fidelity Effort
Notion AI agent Business or Enterprise plan High — headings, tables, lists rebuilt Low, just a prompt
Your own AI via MCP Any Notion plan + an AI client High — comparable to the native agent Medium, one-time setup
PDF-then-convert Any Notion plan Variable — inherits PDF layout quirks Low, but may need cleanup

Final thoughts

Getting a Notion page into Word format is no longer the awkward copy-paste job it used to be, but the export is still just the starting point. Whichever method produces the DOCX, what happens after matters just as much: opening it in ONLYOFFICE Document Editor turns a static export back into a document a team can actually keep working on together.

author: Alice
contentHtml:
Summary

A hanging indent is a paragraph format where the first line is flush left while every subsequent line is indented inward. This style is particularly useful for bibliographies, glossaries, and legal citations, as it visually distinguishes the first line from the rest of the entry, making it easier to read and reference.

  • A hanging indent keeps the first line flush left.
  • It's commonly used in bibliographies and reference lists.
  • To create one in ONLYOFFICE, use paragraph settings.
  • Avoid manual tabs or spaces for consistent formatting.
  • Check your style guide for the correct indent value.

When formatting a bibliography, a glossary, or a list of legal citations by hand (hitting Tab, hitting Enter, hitting Tab again for every single entry) a hanging indent is the fix you’ve been missing. Instead of indenting the first line of a paragraph, a hanging indent pushes in every line except the first, keeping the opening word flush left while the rest of the entry wraps neatly underneath. This guide covers what a hanging indent is, when to use it, and how to set one up.

What is a hanging indent?

A hanging indent (also called a “second-line indent”) is a paragraph format where the first line starts at the left margin and every subsequent line is indented inward. It’s the mirror image of a standard first-line indent, which pushes only the opening line inward and leaves the rest flush left.

Example:

Smith, J. (2024). The history of typography.

Oxford University Press.

The author’s name stays visible at the left edge, and the rest of the citation wraps beneath it. That visual anchor is exactly what makes hanging indents so common in reference lists.

How hanging indents work: The mechanics

A hanging indent is controlled by two separate paragraph settings, not by manual tabs or spaces:

  • First line indent: set to 0, so the first line sits at the paragraph’s left margin.
  • Indent (left): set to a positive value, which shifts the paragraph’s overall left edge inward.

When the first-line value is negative relative to the paragraph’s left indent, the first line “hangs” back out to the margin while every following line falls at the indented position. This is a paragraph-level property, so it moves and reflows automatically as you edit the text. Unlike a manual indent built from Tab and line breaks, which breaks apart the moment the paragraph rewraps.

How to apply a hanging indent

Now let’s see how to set a hanging indent using ONLYOFFICE Document Editor.

First, select your text

  • Place the cursor inside a single paragraph to format just that one.
  • Select several paragraphs with the mouse to format them all at once.
  • Press Ctrl+A to apply the hanging indent to the entire document.

Then apply the hanging indent using either of these two methods.

Method 1: Paragraph Advanced Settings

  • Right-click the selected text and choose Paragraph Advanced Settings (or use Show advanced settings in the right sidebar).

  • Switch to the Indents & Spacing tab.
  • In the Indents section, open the Special dropdown and select Hanging.

  • Adjust the value in the entry field on the right if needed; the default is 1.27 cm (0.5 inch), which matches most academic citation styles.
  • Click OK to apply.

Method 2: The ruler

Make sure rulers are visible first. They’re shown by default, but if they’ve been hidden, go to View → Rulers to bring them back.

On the left side of the horizontal ruler are three markers:

  • The First Line Indent Marker (upper triangle): sets the offset for the first line only.
  • The Hanging Indent Marker (lower triangle): this is the one you drag to create the hanging indent.
  • The Left Indent Marker (rectangle below the triangles): moves all three markers together, shifting the whole paragraph’s offset from the margin.

Click the triangular Hanging Indent Marker and drag it to the right until you reach the offset you want. If you accidentally grab the rectangular Left Indent Marker instead, just drag the First Line Indent Marker back to the left margin to undo it.

Hanging indents vs. first-line indents: Know the difference

Format First line Following lines Common use
First-line indent Indented Flush left Standard prose paragraphs
Hanging indent Flush left Indented Bibliographies, glossaries, legal citations

Mixing the two up is a common formatting mistake — applying a first-line indent to a reference list, for instance, buries the author’s name in the middle of the line instead of anchoring it at the margin, which is exactly what citation styles are designed to avoid.

When to use a hanging indent

  • Bibliographies and reference lists: APA, MLA, and Chicago style all require hanging indents for works-cited entries.
  • Glossaries and definition lists: the term stays flush left while the definition wraps beneath it.
  • Legal documents: numbered clauses and citations often use hanging indents so clause numbers stay visually distinct.
  • Resumes: job titles or dates flush left, with responsibilities indented underneath.
  • Poetry and scripts: occasionally used for stage directions or line continuations.

Practical considerations

A few practictal tips to keep your text nice and clean:

  • Consistency matters: apply the hanging indent as a paragraph style rather than paragraph-by-paragraph if you’re formatting a long document; that way every entry stays uniform if you later adjust the value.
  • Don’t use spaces or tabs: manually indenting with the spacebar or repeated Tab presses breaks as soon as the text rewraps or the font size changes. The paragraph-level setting is the only version that survives edits.
  • Check your style guide: the standard indent value is 0.5 inch in most Western academic styles, but always confirm against the specific citation style you’re following.
  • Works the same across formats: a hanging indent set in ONLYOFFICE Document Editor is preserved when the file is saved as .docx or .odt, so formatting won’t shift when the document moves between editors.
